samples.summary: New task doc recommends granting the agent GitHub App `Workflows: write`, which would defeat both "unforgeable" ready gates
samples.evidence: The doc added by this change states: "**The follow-up that matters is the permission itself** — grant the App `Workflows: write`" (todo line 83). The panel's own trust model depends on the opposite: `.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml:46-52` says the `workflow_run` trigger "is a SECURITY boundary" precisely because "The agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**`", and mark-ready.mjs:1-14 claims gates 1 and 2 are "UNFORGEABLE" because "the author agent cannot create or forge a CI run" and "Only the reviewer workflow (which has checks:write) can post that check". Both claims are consequences of the App lacking workflow-write. Grant it, and an agent-authored `agent/*` branch can add (a) a workflow file whose `name:` is `CI`, triggered on `push`, producing a run named "CI" with conclusion `success` for its own head SHA — which is exactly what `ciPassed` reads (scripts/agent/mark-ready.mjs:133) — and (b) a push-triggered workflow with `permissions: checks: write` that posts `agent-review-<lens>` check runs with conclusion `success` on the same SHA, satisfying gate 2 via `allRequiredPassed`. Both gates then read as green with zero independent evidence and the promote job flips the PR to ready with the App token. The doc presents the grant as the preferred follow-up with no mention of this consequence; the alternative it offers second (an explicit "the agent does not edit workflow files" policy) is the one that preserves the boundary.

samples.summary: Gate 1's "unforgeable" CI evidence is matched by workflow DISPLAY NAME, not workflow path/id — a branch-added workflow named `CI` forges it, and this change pins the name filter as the invariant
samples.evidence: `ciPassed` selects evidence with `(data.workflow_runs ?? []).filter((r) => r.name === "CI")` and then takes the newest by `created_at` (mark-ready.mjs:133-137). `name` is the run's display name, which is whatever the workflow file's `name:` key says — it is not tied to `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Anyone who can push a branch to the BASE repo can add `.github/workflows/anything.yml` with `name: CI` on `push`; its run is recorded against the same `head_sha`, is newer than the real CI run, and `runs[0].conclusion === "success"` returns true even when the genuine CI run for that SHA failed. That path is not hypothetical for this repo: the panel's own header notes "The agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**`, but an `agent:managed` human PR can" (.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml:51), and `agent:managed` is an opt-in label (line 190) that puts such a PR on the promote path. The new test added here (`scripts/agent/mark-ready.test.mjs:184-209`) elevates this name filter to a pinned security property while only exercising differently-NAMED runs, so it documents the check as sound rather than exposing the same-name forge. `set-state.mjs:226` filters CI the same way. A robust filter would key on `r.path === ".github/workflows/ci.yml"` (or `workflow_id`), which cannot be spoofed by a second file.

samples.summary: The new invocation assertion permits `--allow-no-checks` to be appended to the promote job, silently opting out of mark-ready's fail-closed empty-required-check guard
samples.evidence: mark-ready.mjs:70-77 fails closed on an empty required-check set because "gate 2 (review-panel approval) would pass with no evidence" (`allRequiredPassed(runs, [])` is vacuously true), and the ONLY escape is the `--allow-no-checks` argv flag. The new workflow assertion added here is a substring regex: `assert.match(window, /mark-ready\.mjs "\$PR" --promote --require-checks "\$REQUIRED"/)` (test line 346-350). Appending `--allow-no-checks` to the promote invocation still matches that regex, does not add a `|` (so the no-pipe check at line 363 stays green), and does not change any branch of the parsed `case`. The result: a promote job that flips every gate-passing PR to ready with ZERO review-panel evidence whenever `required_checks` resolves empty, with the whole suite green — and this test file is the designated guard for exactly this cross-file contract. Nothing else in the repo pins it: a repo-wide grep for `allow-no-checks` finds only mark-ready.mjs's own guard and the unit test that exercises the flag directly, never an assertion about the workflow. Fix: assert the invocation does NOT contain `--allow-no-checks` (and ideally that `$REQUIRED` is non-empty at the workflow level).
searchedFor: grep -rn 'allow-no-checks' (whole repo) — only mark-ready.mjs:70/73 and mark-ready.test.mjs:157-158
read scripts/agent/mark-ready.test.mjs in full for any negative assertion on the invocation

samples.summary: The promote job runs the ready-gate script from an unpinned `actions/checkout@v4` with credentials persisted — the only trusted-code checkout in the file that does not pin `ref: main`
samples.evidence: The step the modified block executes (`node ./scripts/agent/mark-ready.mjs`, line 1499) comes from `- uses: actions/checkout@v4 # default branch — only need the gate script` (line 1466). Every other trusted-code checkout in this workflow pins it explicitly: line 344 (`ref: main` + `persist-credentials: false`), line 524 (`ref: main`, path `.trusted`), line 1626 (`ref: main` + `persist-credentials: false`), line 2393 (`ref: main`) — and line 400 deliberately pins the reviewed head SHA, proving the default is not relied on for trust anywhere else. Today the implicit `workflow_run` default resolves to the default branch so this is safe, but the integrity of the gate script (the component that holds `GH_MUTATION_TOKEN` and performs the promotion) rests on that implicit default rather than on an explicit pin; adding a `push`/`pull_request`/`workflow_dispatch` trigger, or a maintainer copying this step, would silently execute branch-supplied gate code with an App token that can mark PRs ready. It also keeps `persist-credentials: true` (the default), leaving GITHUB_TOKEN in `.git/config` on the runner that holds the App token, unlike its siblings.

samples.summary: The exit-1 corroboration is a substring grep over a log that now merges stderr, so log content can mask a crash as the benign "gates said no"
samples.evidence: `1) grep -qF "Not promoting: one or more gates are not satisfied" "$RUNNER_TEMP/mark-ready.log"` (line 1518) decides whether an exit 1 is trusted, and the log is written with `2>&1` (line 1500), so it now contains stderr as well as stdout — including Node's `execFileSync` error messages, which embed the full `gh` argv (e.g. `-f labels[]=<label>` at mark-ready.mjs:232-234, where label names are set by anyone with triage rights) and the child's stderr. Any text on either stream that contains the needle makes a genuine crash (exit 1 from a SyntaxError, a failed import, an unhandled rejection) read as "a gate said no": the step echoes "leaving as draft", the job SUCCEEDS, and no page is raised — the exact silent-stall failure this block exists to remove. I could not complete an end-to-end exploit (the label-warning path exits 0, not 1, so the needle and the crash have to coincide by another route), hence low confidence. A signal the script controls exclusively — e.g. requiring the verdict on the LAST line, or having mark-ready write a machine-readable verdict file the workflow reads — would not be spoofable by log content at all. Note also that no promotion can result from this; the impact is a silenced failure, not a bypass.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element verified. The task doc at lines 82-84 does recommend granting the agent App `Workflows: write` (listed first, under a bolded "The follow-up that matters is the permission itself"), with no mention of the security consequence — the doc frames the missing permission purely as developer friction (lines 55-79). The boundary it would break is documented in this repo: agent-review-panel.yml:46-52 states `workflow_run` "is a SECURITY boundary" because it runs the default-branch definition and "The agent App cannot push `.github/workflows/**`", and mark-ready.mjs:1-14 calls gates 1 and 2 "UNFORGEABLE" on the same premise. The exploit chain is unguarded in code: gate 1 is a bare name match (`mark-ready.mjs:133` `r.name === "CI"`, then `conclusion === "success"` at :137) with no workflow-path/id/actor verification, and gate 2 is a bare check-run name match (`mark-ready.mjs:151-155` → `checks.mjs:41-52`) with no app-id verification. So with workflow-write, an agent branch could ship a push-triggered workflow named `CI` plus one with `permissions: checks: write` posting `agent-review-<lens>` successes on its own head SHA, turning both gates green with zero independent evidence and letting `promote` flip the PR to ready. I considered refuting as out-of-scope since this is prose rather than code, but declined: weakened permission gates are squarely in the security lane, this doc is harness policy, and the recommendation targets the exact permission both unforgeability claims rest on.

verdict.reason: The claimed code exists verbatim: mark-ready.mjs:133-137 selects CI evidence with `filter((r) => r.name === "CI")` and takes the newest by created_at, and the header at mark-ready.mjs:4-10 declares that gate "UNFORGEABLE". `name` is the workflow's display name, not tied to .github/workflows/ci.yml (ci.yml:4 is the only file currently named "CI"), so a second branch-added workflow file with `name: CI` produces a run against the same head_sha that sorts first and satisfies gate 1 even when the real CI run failed. No guard elsewhere closes it: the fork exclusion at agent-review-panel.yml:156-160 blocks outside contributors but not a base-repo branch, and the panel's own header at agent-review-panel.yml:50-52 states that an `agent:managed` human PR (opt-in label, line 190) CAN push .github/workflows/**, i.e. the repo's own threat model treats this capability as adversarial. The workflow_run trigger and default-branch checkout (agent-review-panel.yml:26-53, 1466) protect checks:write and the gate script, not which run ciPassed reads; the upstream `ci` job (lines 277-327) waits on the triggering run id, which is itself name-matched (line 28), so it does not re-anchor the evidence either. set-state.mjs:226 repeats the same name-keyed selection, and the new test at mark-ready.test.mjs:184-209 pins the name filter as correct while only exercising differently-named runs. Impact is bounded (the pipeline never merges; promotion only flips draft to ready), which keeps this at major rather than critical, but it is a real forgeable-evidence weakness in an explicitly security-load-bearing gate, so I have no ground to refute.

verdict.reason: The literal absence is real — no test asserts the promote invocation lacks `--allow-no-checks` — but it is not a security defect under this lens. (1) The guard is enforced today: mark-ready.mjs:70-77 fails closed, and the single invocation site (.github/workflows/agent-review-panel.yml:1499-1500) passes only `--promote --require-checks "$REQUIRED"`; a repo-wide grep finds `allow-no-checks` nowhere in any workflow. The claimed impact requires a source edit to trusted main that does not exist. (2) The flag is inert without an empty required set, and that precondition is independently pinned against the real manifest: lenses.json:3-36 keeps correctness and security at gating "blocking" / appliesWhen ["**"], and review-panel.test.mjs:1424-1446 plus 1221-1230 fail the suite if any diff could yield an empty blocking-lens set (workflow line 963 builds `required` from blocking && applicable lenses). Two tested invariants would have to break together. (3) No attacker-controlled path: the promote job checks out the default branch (yml:1466) and the workflow file itself comes from trusted main, so a PR-side edit cannot affect that PR's own promotion — it needs a human merge, itself reviewed by the blocking `**`-scoped security lens. (4) The outcome is draft→ready, not merge, which remains behind branch protection (mark-ready.mjs:22-25). What is left is the tightness of one regression-guard regex — the test-adequacy lane, explicitly deferred by this rubric, and at most hardening rather than a blocking vulnerability.
